readerTitle: Four choices that make or break a team bonus
caseNote: 가상 시뮬레이션 (배관·난방 수리 회사: 가정 수리팀 + 사무실 건물 유지보수 계약팀) · 모든 수치와 인물은 설명용
insight: 팀 보너스는 금액보다 설계가 중요하다. 누구에게, 어떤 숫자로, 어떻게 나누고, 언제 보여 주는지 네 가지 선택이 행동을 바꾼다.
misconception: 보너스는 많이 주기만 하면 성과가 오른다. 매출처럼 측정하기 쉬운 숫자 하나에 걸면 충분하다.

sources.text: 보상 설계의 일반 원칙 (팀 vs 개인 인센티브, 상충 지표, 절차 공정성, 보상 시점)
모든 인물, 회사, 수치는 설명용 가상 사례

factChecks.note: 모든 수치는 설명용 가상 수치입니다. 연간 보너스 예산 $30,000 ÷ 4분기 = 분기당 $7,500으로 카드 4의 금액과 맞습니다.
'규칙을 미리 알면 분배를 더 잘 받아들인다'는 절차 공정성 연구의 일반적 결론을 단순화한 문장입니다. 특정 연구 수치는 인용하지 않았습니다. PPL-04-03 레슨의 표현과 일치하는지 확인하세요.
테크니션 대사와 1분기 변화는 가상 장면입니다. 실제 결과처럼 읽히지 않도록 'Say you chose' 표현과 illustrative 라벨을 유지했습니다.

cards.title: Four choices that make or break a team bonus
body: Dana runs a plumbing and heating company with 12 technicians. Half fix homes. Half service office buildings on yearly contracts.

Last year she paid commission on every job. Revenue rose. So did angry calls. Techs grabbed quick, well-paid jobs and left messy ones for whoever was last at the yard. Free return visits to fix rushed work kept climbing.
This year Dana has **$30,000** for a team bonus instead. You're helping her design it.

image.label: Plumbing vans at a yard, one messy job ticket left on the board
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 아침의 작업장 마당에 수리 밴 여러 대. 게시판에 작업 티켓이 붙어 있고, 깔끔한 티켓들은 모두 떼어졌는데 얼룩진 '복잡한 작업' 티켓 하나만 남아 있음. 실제 회사 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Who should the bonus reward?
body: Home and office crews share one dispatcher and one fleet of vans. On busy days they cover for each other.

options.text: Each technician, based on their own jobs
options.feedback: You keep the hustle, and the cherry-picking. Nobody gains by taking the hard job or helping a colleague finish.

options.text: Each crew separately: one pool for home, one for offices
options.feedback: Each crew pulls together. But lending a tech to the other crew now shrinks your own pool, so busy days get worse.

options.text: One pool for the whole company
options.feedback: The work is shared, so the reward is too. Covering for a colleague now helps your bonus. The risk is that some people coast.

cards.title: What number decides the size of the pool?
body: Say you chose one company-wide pool. Now pick the number that makes it grow or shrink.

options.feedback: Easy to track, but it rewards upselling and rushing. Last year's problem comes back, just shared.

options.text: Profit on jobs after parts and labor, minus the cost of every free return visit
options.feedback: Profit pushes efficient work. Subtracting return visits makes rushed work cost the pool. Two numbers that pull against each other are harder to game.
It points at quality. But reviews about prices or wait times, which techs don't control, can swing it.

cards.title: How do you split it?
body: Say you chose profit minus return visits. The first quarter ends well: the pool is $7,500.
Two techs work part-time. One is an apprentice on lower pay.

options.feedback: Simple, and it feels united. But full-timers notice that someone working half the hours gets the same share.

options.text: In proportion to each person's base pay
options.feedback: It looks neutral, but the best-paid get the most from a result everyone built. The apprentice learns that rank beats effort.

options.text: In proportion to hours worked, with the rule shared before the quarter starts
options.feedback: Effort and reward line up, and nobody is surprised. People accept a split more easily when they knew the rule in advance.

cards.title: When and how do people see it?
body: Say you chose to split by hours. One question left: timing.

options.text: Pay it all in one lump at year end
options.feedback: A big payment feels good. But in March, nobody links today's careful repair to money in December.

options.text: Pay quarterly, and post the running pool on a board at the yard each week
options.feedback: People see their work move the number while it still matters. The board also gives Dana a weekly moment to thank whoever saved a return visit.
Fast feedback, but small sums and weather-driven swings make it feel random. One slow month can punish good work.

cards.title: Small habits start to change.
body: Say you chose all four. In the first quarter, techs start calling each other before closing a job: "Did you check the valve under the sink?"
During a cold snap, the office crew lends two people to the home crew, because helping now pays. Hard jobs still aren't popular, but dodging them no longer earns anything.
One tech says the board is the first time he's seen what a return visit **actually costs**.

image.label: Weekly scoreboard at the yard showing the bonus pool growing
image.brief: 작업장 벽에 걸린 화이트보드. 주별 막대가 점점 올라가는 'Team pool' 그래프와 아래쪽에 빨간색 'Return visits −$' 칸. 테크니션 두 명이 커피를 들고 보드를 보며 이야기하는 모습. 실제 로고 없음.

cards.title: A team bonus can't fix everything.
body: **Free riders:** if one person coasts, everyone's pool shrinks and resentment builds. That's a management problem. Deal with it directly, not through the formula.
**Size:** if the bonus becomes a big part of pay, people argue about the formula instead of the work. Keep it meaningful but modest.
**Stability:** keep the rules for at least a year. Changing them every quarter teaches people that the rules are up for negotiation.
cards.softwareNote: The same four choices apply to a software team. A team bonus on new sign-ups invites heavy discounting, so pair it with a counterweight such as customers still paying after 90 days.

cards.title: Design the bonus around the behavior you want.
body: Each decision you made maps to an idea from this unit.
list: **Who:** reward the unit that shares the work, or you pay people to stop helping each other (incentives across teams)
**What:** pair a goal with a counterweight, or people hit the number and miss the point (when incentives backfire)
**How to split:** link shares to effort and publish the rule in advance (fairness)
**When:** pay soon and make progress visible, so money and thanks arrive together (recognition)
cards.callout: **Try it today:** take any bonus or target your business uses. Write down the easiest way someone could hit it while doing worse work. If you can find one, add a counterweight.
